PMGT1852 Week 07

PMGT1852 Week 7 - Self-Awareness and Emotional Intelligence

Why self-awareness matters

Self-awareness is the capacity to recognise one's own emotions, assumptions, values and behaviour, including their effects on others. It is a working capability, not simply introspection. A facilitator or stakeholder manager uses their own judgement and communication as instruments of engagement, so understanding those instruments matters.

Confucius' emphasis on looking within oneself and Lao Tzu's distinction between conquering others and mastering oneself express the same practical orientation: improvement begins by examining one's own contribution to a situation.

The intent-impact gap is the difference between what someone intends to communicate and what others actually experience. A well-intended message can still sound dismissive or threatening. Self-examination and feedback help identify this gap; good intentions alone do not close it.

The navigation analogy makes the starting point concrete. When a person is lost on the way to a friend's house, useful guidance first requires an honest answer to "Where are you now?" Development similarly requires an accurate understanding of present behaviour before choosing how to change it.

Brouwer's growth sequence

Self-examination -> insight -> self-understanding -> changed behaviour

• Self-examination: inspect one's actions, reactions and assumptions.

• Insight: recognise something previously unnoticed.

• Self-understanding: integrate that insight into an account of why one behaves as one does.

• Changed behaviour: act differently in relevant situations.

Insight is a building block, not the final outcome. The practical value of reflection depends on what changes afterwards.

Three foundations of self-awareness

Self-understanding and self-management

Self-concept is the way a person understands themselves. It affects how they interpret others and react to feedback. Self-awareness and self-acceptance support growth and the ability to understand and accept other people; acceptance does not mean treating every behaviour as desirable.

Core self-evaluation concerns a person's fundamental appraisal of themselves. Related components include:

Component

Meaning

Positive self-regard

A broadly accepting view of oneself

Self-esteem

A sense of personal worth

Self-efficacy

Belief in one's capacity to perform a task or handle a situation

Emotional stability

Relative steadiness in emotional responses

Locus of control

Beliefs about the extent to which outcomes depend on one's actions or external forces

These appraisals are relevant to job satisfaction, performance and life satisfaction, but should not be treated as a deterministic causal formula.

The five-factor personality model offers a separate descriptive vocabulary:

• Extraversion: sociability, assertiveness and excitability.

• Openness: imagination, creativity, curiosity and receptiveness to new experiences.

• Conscientiousness: thoughtfulness, impulse control and goal focus.

• Agreeableness: trust, kindness, altruism and cooperation.

• Neuroticism: susceptibility to sadness, moodiness and emotional instability.

Such descriptions support reflection; they are not verdicts on a person's value or a complete prediction of behaviour. Core self-evaluation and the five-factor model describe related but distinct aspects of the person.

Useful objects of self-evaluation include the sensitive line, personal values, attitude towards change, interpersonal style, emotional intelligence and communication-matching capabilities.

The sensitive line

The sensitive line is the point at which information inconsistent with one's self-concept, or pressure to change behaviour, triggers defensiveness or self-protection. Crossing it can produce a threat-rigidity response: perceived threat narrows thinking and encourages rigid defence of the existing position.

Feedback can therefore be reasonable in content yet ineffective in delivery. The recipient may defend their identity instead of examining the information.

Information is less threatening when it is:

• Verifiable: grounded in observations that can be checked.

• Predictable: not delivered as an unexplained surprise or ambush.

• Controllable: connected to behaviour the recipient can influence.

Give observable, specific and repeatable examples rather than sweeping interpretations of character. Sharing experience with a trusted mentor can support insight because difficult information is easier to explore in a relationship of trust.

Understanding and respecting individual differences

Self-awareness involves understanding one's own distinctive strengths and recognising differences in others, within and across cultures. Self-disclosure, sharing and trusting dialogue allow people to test their interpretations rather than relying on private assumptions.

Distinguish describing differences from ranking people through prejudicial distinctions. An observed difference is information; it does not automatically establish that one person or culture is superior.

A homogeneous leadership group can develop structural blind spots when its members approach problems in similar ways. Diversity can introduce alternative perspectives, provided those perspectives influence decisions rather than merely being present.

Five dimensions of self-awareness

1. Values

Values are enduring beliefs about what matters and what is desirable. They underpin attitudes and preferences and develop through experience, family, country, ethnicity and tradition. They are relatively stable, not necessarily unchangeable.

Seven cultural-value contrasts provide a vocabulary for examining assumptions:

Dimension

Contrast

Universalism / particularism

General rules versus attention to particular relationships and circumstances

Individualism / collectivism

Individual autonomy versus group obligations and identity

Affective / neutral

More open versus more restrained emotional expression

Specific / diffuse

More separate versus more overlapping personal and work relationships

Achievement / ascription

Status associated with accomplishments versus attributed position or identity

Past / present / future

Relative emphasis on tradition, present circumstances or future possibilities

Internal / external control

Emphasis on shaping circumstances versus adapting to external conditions

These contrasts invite enquiry; they do not justify predicting an individual's behaviour from nationality.

Management can emphasise instruction through prescribed actions, objectives through desired results, or values through shared principles. Managers face value conflicts between economic performance, such as costs and profit, and social performance, such as employee and customer satisfaction.

Instrumental values concern preferred means of acting; terminal values concern desired end states. A project disagreement may concern how to deliver, what to deliver, or both.

2. Interpersonal style

Interpersonal style is a recurring way of influencing and communicating with other people. Recognising one's cultural values and communication behaviour helps build effective working relationships.

The Leadership Enhancement Team Style (LETS) framework emphasises the importance of non-verbal behaviour. Matching aspects of another person's non-verbal communication can increase a sense of similarity and support communication. This does not establish a fixed percentage of meaning carried by non-verbal signals.

Team leadership role

Typical emphasis

Planner

Planning, monitoring and coordinating to make things happen

Analyser

Methods, procedures, rules and quality

Developer

Pursuing opportunities and expanding the project

Creator

Innovative problem-solving, energy and enthusiasm

These are roles and tendencies, not fixed personality identities.

Communication differences can be described along six continua:

• Rapid / gradual.

• Exaggerated / understated.

• Linear / lateral.

• Detail / concept.

• Self-evaluation / evaluation by others.

• Initiating / responding.

A related perceptual vocabulary distinguishes visual, auditory and experiential ways of representing experience. Such labels describe preferences and should not become judgements about ability.

Named comparison instruments include the Herrmann Brain Dominance Instrument; DISC, a behavioural-style framework commonly described through dominance, influence, steadiness and conscientiousness; the Strong Interest Inventory; the Sixteen Personality Factor Questionnaire (16PF); the Kolb Learning Style Inventory (LSI); the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator (MBTI); and the Honey and Mumford Learning Styles Questionnaire (LSQ). Naming an instrument does not establish its validity for every personnel or development decision.

3. Emotional intelligence

Emotional intelligence (EI) concerns recognising and managing emotions in oneself and in relationships. Emotional quotient (EQ) is often used as a related measurement label. Emotions affect decision-making, problem-solving and conflict; they are part of work rather than irrelevant noise around it.

A practical four-capability account is:

Identify and diagnose one's own emotions.

Regulate one's own emotions.

Recognise emotional signals in others.

Respond appropriately to those signals.

These capabilities can develop through learning and practice. They should not be treated as wholly fixed at birth, nor should development be taken to mean that biological and individual differences have no role.

Intelligence quotient (IQ) concerns measured cognitive ability and is distinct from EI. High cognitive ability alone does not guarantee effective relationships, happiness or leadership. Conversely, that distinction does not establish that cognitive ability is irrelevant to performance.

Strong emotional capabilities can support accurate recognition of feelings, more appropriate emotional expression, empathy and stress management. Associations with positive outcomes do not mean that EI prevents anxiety or depression or substitutes for mental-health care.

4. Attitude towards change

Change is a continuing feature of organisational life. Openness or defensiveness towards change affects how people receive information and communicate it to others.

Locus of control describes beliefs about the causes of outcomes or reinforcement:

• Internal: outcomes are interpreted as depending substantially on one's actions.

• External: outcomes are interpreted as depending substantially on outside forces.

These beliefs can influence willingness to take ownership of a problem. They are not proof that a particular outcome is actually controllable, or that someone with an external orientation will always remain passive.

5. Cognitive style

Cognitive style concerns how a person gathers, interprets, evaluates and responds to information. Two relevant preference dimensions are:

Dimension

One preference

Contrasting preference

Gathering information

Intuition: overall patterns, possibilities and the whole

Sensing: concrete observations, details and parts

Evaluating information

Thinking: explicit logic and consistency

Feeling: values and implications for people

These information-gathering and evaluation dimensions are associated with the MBTI framework. Their combinations produce four preference pairings, not a complete account of its full type system. A feeling preference should not simply be equated with irrationality, and neither preference excludes logic or emotion. Preference is not competence.

The ladder of inference

Raw observations -> selected data -> added meanings -> assumptions -> conclusions -> beliefs -> action

People do not act on an unfiltered copy of reality. They select some observations, interpret them, make assumptions and develop conclusions. Existing beliefs can then influence what they notice next.

Two people may disagree about an action because their earlier selection or interpretation of information differs. To investigate a disagreement, ask what each observed, what meaning they attached to it and what assumptions connect that meaning to their conclusion. Arguing only about the final conclusion may leave the underlying difference untouched.

Goleman's four EI domains

Goleman describes EI as how well people handle themselves and their relationships.

Domain

Meaning

Self-awareness

Recognising what one feels and why; understanding emotional and value signals relevant to judgement

Self-management

Handling distressing emotions without being overwhelmed, learning from them and mobilising positive emotions such as enthusiasm

Empathy

Understanding what others feel

Relationship capability

Integrating the other capabilities into effective interactions

Every emotion can have a function. Self-management is not emotional suppression: it involves responding constructively to emotional information.

Development and neurological reasoning

Neuroplasticity is the brain's capacity to change with experience. Emotional and social capabilities develop over time, and repeated practice can strengthen relevant patterns of behaviour. The neurological argument for sustained social-emotional learning is therefore stronger than the idea of a single isolated training event.

Executive functions are capacities involved in directing attention and regulating behaviour. Prefrontal brain systems contribute to these functions as well as aspects of emotional regulation. This provides a mechanism through which social-emotional learning may also support learning more generally; it is not proof of a single simple pathway for every outcome.

Reported educational findings

A meta-analysis combines findings from multiple studies. Goleman's account of school social-emotional learning comparisons describes reduced antisocial behaviour and classroom disruption, increased prosocial behaviour, and improved academic achievement. Prosocial behaviour means behaviour that benefits others.

These findings support the possibility that emotional and social development can benefit both relationships and learning. Benefits vary with the programme, participants and context; a combined research finding is not a guaranteed outcome for an individual school or project.

Leadership, gender and culture

Emotionally destructive management can undermine an organisation's own mission. The practical implication of managing with care is to recognise that the quality of relationships affects what the organisation can accomplish.

A long-term rise in measured IQ does not establish a corresponding rise in EI. Conflict, hatred and domestic abuse illustrate concern about emotional regulation, but they do not by themselves constitute a valid time series proving that population EI has declined.

Goleman's account describes average differences in particular capabilities: women showing stronger emotional empathy and social capabilities on average, and men showing greater group self-confidence and management of distressing emotions on average. The same account reports no differences on these variables among the top 10% of leaders. These observations do not determine an individual's ability and should not become gender-based selection rules.

EI can be broadly relevant across cultures while being expressed through different local conventions. Japanese social interaction may rely on subtle rules unfamiliar to outsiders; more openly expressive settings, such as the Brazilian and Italian examples, can look different. Effective engagement requires learning local meanings rather than mistaking unfamiliar expression for an absence of emotional capability.

Reflection, bias and inclusion

Consider a team member who dismisses stakeholders because of their formal roles, resists peers' evidence of informal influence and gives greater weight to numerical or fluent-English contributions.

Confirmation bias means favouring information that supports an existing belief while discounting conflicting evidence. Defending a judgement alone is not enough to diagnose it; examine how evidence is selected and assessed.

Risk

Corrective action

Mechanism

Overlooking informal influence

Revisit stakeholder classifications using peers' evidence of actual relationships

Tests role-based assumptions against relevant evidence

Dominant voices shaping the discussion

Use structured turn-taking

Makes room for contributions that might otherwise be crowded out

Confirmation bias

Explicitly seek dissenting views and pause before judging new information

Creates an opportunity to reconsider assumptions

Cultural or presentation bias

Review whose ideas actually influenced the decision

Tests whether inclusion affected outcomes rather than merely attendance

Rank, fluent English and numerical presentation are not automatic evidence of superior insight. Reflection becomes useful when it changes behaviour and engagement decisions.
